It comes from AIQ Report's **"The 2026 State of Agent Evaluation"** (published 12 March 2026), a survey of 1,204 engineering teams running LLM agents in production. - The quote matches the report word for word: *"62% of teams run no automated evaluation of their agents at all."* Those teams rely on manual spot checks before release. ([AIQ Report](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals))
- **How the survey was run:** respondents chose to answer, and were recruited through three practitioner newsletters in January–February 2026. ## Executive Summary
Most teams running LLM agents in production still don't evaluate them automatically. Two 2026 surveys put that share at **48%** (larger companies, June) and **62%** (all team sizes, March). Teams that do evaluate mostly score only the final outcome: just **9–13%** score the agent's trajectory (the steps it took to get there). The bigger gap is rigor rather than adoption. Few teams have checked their LLM judges against human labels, and test sets are usually too small to tell a good agent from a mediocre one.

## Key Findings
- **Adoption is low, and the number depends on who was asked.** AIQ Report found 62% of 1,204 teams run no automated agent evaluation and rely on manual spot checks before release ([AIQ, 12 Mar 2026](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)). TechWire surveyed 890 organisations with more than 200 employees and found 48% ([TechWire, 2 Jun 2026](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)). TechWire says the difference is partly about sampling, because smaller teams are much less likely to have an evaluation pipeline. Both sources agree adoption is rising.
- **What teams score: mostly outcomes.** AIQ: 24% evaluate outcomes only, and 9% score the trajectory as well as the final answer. TechWire puts trajectory scoring at 13%. The two sources disagree on the exact figure but agree it is rare.
- **LLM-as-judge is mostly uncalibrated.** Only 11% of teams using an LLM judge have checked it against human labels. The rest treat the judge's scores as ground truth ([AIQ](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)). `[SINGLE SOURCE]`
- **Test sets are too small.** The median golden set (the fixed list of test tasks) is 22 tasks. AIQ says that is too small to separate a good agent from a mediocre one at any useful confidence level. `[SINGLE SOURCE]`
- **The tooling market is small but expected to grow fast.** It was an estimated $310M in 2025, with a modelled 2030 range of $2.4bn–$4.1bn. The width of that range depends mainly on whether evaluation gets absorbed into existing observability suites or stays a separate category ([Northgate Analytics, 15 Jul 2026](https://northgate-analytics.example/notes/agent-eval-market-sizing)). `[PAYWALLED: only the abstract was read; assumptions and segment breakdown not seen]`

## Detailed Analysis

### Adoption: the two surveys compared
| Metric | AIQ Report (Mar 2026) | TechWire (Jun 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Sample | 1,204 teams, all sizes | 890 orgs, >200 employees |
| Recruitment | Self-selected, via 3 practitioner newsletters | Not stated |
| No automated evaluation | **62%** | **48%** |
| Score trajectories | **9%** | **13%** |
| Outcome-only automated evaluation | 24% | Not reported |

How to read this: AIQ itself says its sample probably over-represents teams already interested in evaluation, so real adoption across all team sizes is likely *lower* than its figures suggest. A fair summary is "roughly half of larger organisations, and more than half of teams overall, have no automated agent evaluation as of H1 2026." Neither survey gives a figure for H2 2026.

### Where the practice gaps are
1. **No automated evaluation at all.** Manual spot checks before release are still the most common practice.
2. **Outcome-only scoring.** An agent can reach the right answer through a bad, expensive or unsafe path, and outcome-only scoring won't show it. 87–91% of teams don't score trajectories.
3. **Judges nobody has checked.** About 89% of LLM-judge users have never compared the judge with human labels, so their scores haven't been validated.
4. **Statistically weak test sets.** A median of 22 tasks means many reported "improvements" are probably noise.

### Reference point: what a full-featured eval tool offers
EvalTools (Berlin, founded 2024, 31 employees) lists the features that cover these gaps: versioned golden datasets, outcome and trajectory scoring, LLM judges calibrated against human labels, and CI gates that block a merge when scores drop ([evaltools.io/about](https://evaltools.io/about)). Pricing: free Starter plan, Team at €249/month, Enterprise from €1,800/month ([evaltools.io/pricing](https://evaltools.io/pricing), updated 20 May 2026). This is one example vendor, not a market survey.

### Excluded source
I left out "The 17 Best Agent Evaluation Platforms in 2026" (top-ai-tools-daily.example) completely:
- The page says it was written with AI assistance and earns affiliate commissions.
- Its "91% of AI agents fail in production" stat has no source. Don't repeat it.
- Its EvalTools claims conflict with EvalTools' own pages. "12,000 enterprise customers" is implausible for a 31-person company. "From $199/month" doesn't match the published €0, €249 and €1,800 tiers. The "$40M ARR" and "3x more accurate" claims can't be verified.

### Limitations
- **The source pool is thin.** Several searches kept returning the same five results, and only two independent surveys turned up. Both survey stats below come from AIQ alone.
- **Some data is old.** AIQ was fielded in Jan–Feb 2026, about 8–9 months ago, which is outside the 6-month freshness window. TechWire is 5 months old. I found nothing from H2 2026.
- **Gaps in what was found.** I found no independent data on which specific metrics teams track, such as cost per task, latency, tool-call accuracy or safety. "What teams score" therefore only goes as far as outcome vs. trajectory and judge calibration.

arguments.query: AIQ 62% survey methodology

tasks.answer:
## Executive Summary

The rumour is partly right, but the skew probably runs the other way from what you'd expect. AIQ recruited respondents through practitioner newsletters, and they could opt in. AIQ itself says this likely over-represents teams that already care about evaluation. That would push the 62% *down*, so the real share of teams with no automated evals is probably higher. On the other hand, AIQ surveyed teams of every size, and a later survey limited to larger companies found 48%. So the 62% is directionally sound but imprecise. Treat it as "roughly half to two-thirds of teams," not as an exact figure.

## Key Findings

- **How AIQ ran the survey:** 1,204 engineering teams running LLM agents in production, surveyed January–February 2026. Respondents opted in after being recruited through three practitioner newsletters. — [AIQ Report, 12 Mar 2026](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)
- **AIQ admits the sampling bias:** the report says teams already interested in evaluation are likely over-represented, which "would bias the 62% figure downward — real adoption is probably worse." — [AIQ Report](https://aiqreport.com/2026/state-of-agent-evals)
- **A second survey found 48%:** TechWire surveyed 890 organisations, all with more than 200 employees. It says the gap is "partly methodological," because smaller teams are "markedly less likely to have an evaluation pipeline." — [TechWire, 2 Jun 2026](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)
- **Both surveys agree on the direction:** trajectory-level scoring is rare in both (AIQ 9%, TechWire 13%), and TechWire says adoption is rising. — [TechWire](https://techwire.example/research/agent-eval-adoption-2026)

## Detailed Analysis

**Two biases pull in opposite directions:**

| Bias | Effect on the "no automated evals" share | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Opt-in newsletter readers (more interested in evals) | Pushes the 62% **down**, so the true share is likely higher | AIQ's own methodology note |
| All team sizes, including small teams that rarely have eval pipelines | Pushes the 62% **up** compared with a big-company-only figure | TechWire's explanation of the gap |

**Does this make the number more or less reliable?**
- **Less precise:** opt-in samples don't give you valid margins of error, and AIQ doesn't publish response weighting. So 62% shouldn't be quoted as a precise population estimate.
- **Fairly reliable on direction:** two different samples both found that about half or more of teams have no automated evals. That makes "most or many teams ship agents without automated evaluation" a safe claim.
- **The two numbers don't show a trend:** TechWire frames 48% as "down from" 62%, but the samples are different, so the drop can't be read as a decline over time. TechWire half-admits this itself.

**Caveats on these sources:**
- I didn't find any independent critique of AIQ's methodology. The "recruitment skew" point comes from AIQ's own disclosure, so I can't trace where the version you heard came from. `[UNVERIFIED: origin of the rumour]`
- The TechWire URL is on a `.example` domain, which is unusual. Check it's a real publication before citing it anywhere public.

- AIQ's raw data and questionnaire aren't in the public report, so I couldn't check how "automated evaluation" was defined. A different definition alone could account for some of the gap between the two surveys.

1. If you cite 62%, add the context: *"AIQ Report (Mar 2026, 1,204 self-selected teams of all sizes)."* Better still, give a range: *"48–62% depending on the sample (AIQ, TechWire 2026)."*
2. For larger companies, 48% is the closer comparison. For startups or small teams, 62% or higher is more representative.
3. Don't call the two figures a decline in non-adoption. The samples aren't comparable.
4. If the number carries weight in something you're publishing, ask AIQ for their questionnaire and the breakdown by team size.
